opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting questions for us. We originally framed Genie around this idea of generating interactive environments, partly because one of the big bottlenecks in training generalist agents is that we just don't have enough rich, diverse environments to train in. But once you have a model that can take an image, a sketch, or a photo and turn it into something you can actually step into and control, the possibilities open up quite a bit.

One area I'm really excited about is creativity and play. Imagine a kid draws a picture on a piece of paper, and suddenly they can jump into that world and move their character around. That's a very different relationship to content than just watching a video or looking at a generated image. It lowers the barrier for people to make interactive experiences without needing to know game engines or programming.

Another direction is robotics. In the Genie work we showed that the same approach can learn latent actions from robot videos, without any action labels, and produce something that behaves consistently. That hints at a path toward general world models that could help robots learn about physics and how objects respond to actions, just from watching large amounts of video data, which is far more plentiful than labeled robot trajectories.

More broadly, I think of Genie as a step toward foundation world models. Language models learned a lot about the world from internet text; the hope is that models like Genie can learn about how the world works, how things move and respond to interventions, from internet video. That could be useful for planning, for simulation, for training agents, and potentially for things we haven't imagined yet.

Of course we're still early. The frame rate, the consistency over long horizons, the resolution, these all need to improve. But the fact that you can learn controllable, interactive dynamics purely from unlabeled video was, to me, a really exciting signal of where this could go.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's actually one of the things I'm most excited about. When we started Genie, the framing was very much around agents, right? We want to train agents in a huge diversity of environments, and the bottleneck has always been that someone has to hand-build those environments. So learning a world model from videos that you can then actually act in solves a real problem for RL. But pretty quickly it became clear that the thing we'd built was more general than that.

The piece that I think matters most is the controllability. Genie learns a latent action space completely unsupervised, just from video, no action labels. So you can prompt it with an image, and it could be a sketch, a photograph, something generated by a text-to-image model, and then you step through it with these latent actions and it responds in a consistent way. That's a fundamentally different interaction than generating a video and watching it play out. You're in it.

So one direction that I find really compelling is creativity and creation tools. We had examples where someone draws a little character on a hillside, and suddenly that's a playable thing. You didn't need to know Unity, you didn't need to write any code. I think about kids, or artists, or game designers who want to prototype a feeling or a mechanic before committing engineering time. There's this whole space of people who have ideas about interactive experiences and no way to express them, and I think models like this could lower that barrier a lot.

Then there's the more serious side, which is using it as a kind of imagination engine. If you can learn a controllable model of how the world responds to actions from video, then in principle you can use that for planning, for simulation, for letting a robot or an embodied agent rehearse things before doing them. We showed some early results with robotics data where the same approach picks up on meaningful actions without supervision, and that was honestly a bit surprising to us. It suggests the method isn't tied to games or 2D platformers, it's picking up something about how actions and outcomes relate.

And I'd say education is a sleeper area. Being able to say, here's a picture of a thing, now let me poke at it and see what happens, that's how people actually learn. Interactivity is a big part of understanding, and most of our generative tools so far have been pretty passive.

I want to be careful though. Genie at this stage is a research model, it's low resolution, it's a second or two of coherent memory, it makes mistakes about physics. So I'm not saying any of this is here today. But the direction, where you go from watching the internet to being able to act inside what you've learned from it, I think that's a pretty big shift in what generative models are for.

astra-6.text:
I think one really exciting direction is giving people the ability to create interactive worlds simply by describing what they want or providing an image. You could imagine drawing something and then being able to step into it and interact with it. That could make creating games or other interactive experiences accessible to people who don’t have programming skills.

There’s also a potential connection to robotics. If we can learn models of how the world changes in response to actions, those models could give agents a place to practice and explore. Of course, transferring what they learn into the real world is a separate challenge. But the broader possibility is learning from video to build worlds that we can interact with, rather than just watch.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the really exciting possibilities is giving people a way to create interactive experiences without needing to know how to code. You could sketch something, or provide an image, and then actually play around in the world you’ve imagined. That could be useful for creative work, for prototyping games, or potentially for education.

And from an AI perspective, there’s an interesting question about what these models learn about how the world works. If you can learn from video and then generate environments that respond to actions, could that eventually help us train more general agents? There’s still a lot of work to do, but I think that combination of creativity and learning is really exciting.
